data.title: Language-Interference Errors in Claimed-Native Content
data.summary:
Content presented as written by a native speaker carries repeated, patterned spelling
and grammar deviations consistent with interference from a specific other first
language, rather than the one-off slips a genuine native speaker makes.
data.description:
Every author makes mistakes; a native speaker's are scattered and random. A systematic
error — the same false friend chosen every time, the same idiom calqued literally from
another language, a gender or article agreement mistake that only a speaker of a
gendered-noun language would make, a loanword spelled the way the source language spells
it rather than the way the claimed language does — is not noise. It is interference from
whatever language the author actually thinks in, and it repeats because the author does
not perceive it as an error.

The diagnostic value is in the pattern, not the individual mistake. One wrong preposition
is a typo; the same wrong preposition in the same construction across a dozen bylines
that are not supposed to share an author is a production chain writing in a language
that is not its own, possibly through light editing of machine translation rather than
raw output — which is why this tell often co-occurs with keyboard-locale punctuation
tells. Either way, the content is less locally produced than it claims to be.

This is a hypothesis about a production chain's working language, not a claim about any
individual's nationality, and forensic linguistics of this kind is suggestive rather than
conclusive even when the pattern is strong. Naming a specific source language or region in
a final report deserves a second opinion from someone who actually speaks it — a pattern
that looks diagnostic to a non-speaker is sometimes just an unusual but valid construction.
data.recommendation:
* Build a glossary of the recurring errors across the corpus — the specific word, the
  specific construction, the specific accounts or bylines it appears under — before
  treating any of it as signal.
* Require the pattern to repeat across content that is not supposed to share an author;
  a single deviation stays an individual's mistake.
* Get a fluent or native reviewer of the candidate source language to confirm the pattern
  reads as interference before it is named in the report, rather than relying on a
  non-speaker's intuition.
* Weigh the finding alongside the corpus's other attribution indicators rather than
  naming a region on linguistic grounds alone, and carry the same confidence caveat the
  attribution section applies to every other hypothesis.
* Hold back the glossary of specific tells from anything published; it is a style guide
  for the next draft.
data.short_recommendation: Build a glossary of recurring, patterned errors and get native-speaker review before naming a source language.
